traditional software development. For decades, code has been king \u2014 specifications were just scaffolding we built and discarded once the \"real work\" of coding began. Spec-Driven Development changes this: **specifications become executable**, directly generating working implementations rather than just guiding them.\n\n## \u26a1 Get Started\n\n### 1. You can use it to see the programs that have a file open, or to see the object types and names of all the handles of a program.\\n\\nYou can also get a GUI-based version of this program, [_Process Explorer_](process-explorer), here at Sysinternals.\\n\\n## Installation\\n\\nYou run _Handle_ by typing \"handle\". You must have administrative privilege to run _Handle_.\\n\\n## Usage\\n\\n_Handle_ is targeted at searching for open file references, so if you do not specify any command-line parameters it will list the values of all the handles in the system that refer to open files and the names of the files. It also takes several parameters that modify this behavior.\\n\\n**usage:** `handle [[-a [-l]] [-v|-vt] [-u] | [-c <handle> [-y]] | [-s]] [-p <process>|<pid>] [name]`\\n\\n| Parameter | Description |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| **\\\\-a** | Dump information about all types of handles, not just those that refer to files. Other types include ports, Registry keys, synchronization primitives, threads, and processes. |\\n| **\\\\-l** | Just show pagefile-backed section handles. |\\n| **\\\\-c** | Closes the specified handle (interpreted as a hexadecimal number). You must specify the process by its PID.  \\n**WARNING:** Closing handles can cause application or system instability. |\\n| **\\\\-g** | Print granted access. |\\n| **\\\\-y** | Don\\'t prompt for close handle confirmation. |\\n| **\\\\-s** | Print count of each type of handle open. |\\n| **\\\\-u** | Show the owning user name when searching for handles. |\\n| **\\\\-v** | CSV output with comma delimiter. |\\n| **\\\\-vt** | CSV output with tab delimiter. |\\n| **\\\\-p** | Instead of examining all the handles in the system, this parameter narrows Handle\\'s scan to those processes that begin with the name process. Thus:  \\n**handle -p exp**  \\nwould dump the open files for all processes that start with \"exp\", which would include Explorer. |\\n| **name** | This parameter is present so that you can direct Handle to search for references to an object with a particular name.  \\nFor example, if you wanted to know which process (if any) has \"c:\\\\\\\\windows\\\\\\\\system32\" open you could type:  \\n**handle windows\\\\\\\\system**  \\nThe name match is c\\n\\n\u2026[truncated \u2014 use ctx_search() for full content]'}]"}

The toolkit includes templates, scripts, and workflows that guide development teams through a structured approach to building software.\\n\\n**Specify CLI** is the command-line interface that bootstraps projects with the Spec Kit framework. It sets up the necessary directory structures, templates, and AI agent integrations to support the Spec-Driven Development workflow.\\n\\nThe toolkit supports multiple AI coding assistants, allowing teams to use their preferred tools while maintaining consistent project structure and development practices.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Integration Architecture\\n\\nEach AI agent is a self-contained **integration subpackage** under `src/specify_cli/integrations/<key>/`. The subpackage exposes a single class that declares all metadata and inherits setup/teardown logic from a base class. Built-in integrations are then instantiated and added to the global `INTEGRATION_REGISTRY` by `src/specify_cli/integrations/__init__.py` via `_register_builtins()`.\\n\\n```\\nsrc/specify_cli/integrations/\\n\\u251c\\u2500\\u2500 __init__.py            # INTEGRATION_REGISTRY + _register_builtins()\\n\\u251c\\u2500\\u2500 base.py                # IntegrationBase, MarkdownIntegration, TomlIntegration, YamlIntegration, SkillsIntegration\\n\\u251c\\u2500\\u2500 manifest.py            # IntegrationManifest (file tracking)\\n\\u251c\\u2500\\u2500 claude/                # Example: SkillsIntegration subclass\\n\\u2502   \\u2514\\u2500\\u2500 __init__.py        #   ClaudeIntegration class\\n\\u251c\\u2500\\u2500 gemini/                # Example: TomlIntegration subclass\\n\\u2502   \\u2514\\u2500\\u2500 __init__.py\\n\\u251c\\u2500\\u2500 windsurf/              # Example: MarkdownIntegration subclass\\n\\u2502   \\u2514\\u2500\\u2500 __init__.py\\n\\u251c\\u2500\\u2500 copilot/               # Example: IntegrationBase subclass (custom setup)\\n\\u2502   \\u2514\\u2500\\u2500 __init__.py\\n\\u2514\\u2500\\u2500 ...                    # One subpackage per supported agent\\n```\\n\\nThe registry is the **single source of truth for Python integration metadata**. Supported agents, their directories, formats, capabilities, and context files are derived from the integration classes for the Python integration layer.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Adding a New Integration\\n\\n### 1. Choose a base class\\n\\n| Your agent needs\\u2026 | Subclass |\\n|---|---|\\n| Standard markdown commands (`.md`) | `MarkdownIntegration` |\\n| TOML-format commands (`.toml`) | `TomlIntegration` |\\n| YAML recipe files (`.yaml`) | `YamlIntegration` |\\n| Skill directories (`speckit-<name>/SKILL.md`) | `SkillsIntegration` |\\n| Fully custom output (companion files, settings merge, etc.) | `IntegrationBase` directly |\\n\\nMost agents only need `MarkdownIntegration` \\u2014 a minimal subclass with zero method overrides.\\n\\n### 2. The `IntegrationBase.key` class attribute always retains the original hyphenated value, since that is what the CLI and registry use. For CLI-based integrations (`requires_cli: True`), the `key` should match the actual CLI tool name (the executable users install and run) so CLI checks can resolve it correctly.
